title: The repaired chair
bodyMd:
A museum's damaged chair presents an apparently simple choice: restore its original appearance or preserve the material that survives. In practice, the two aims can conflict. Replacing a missing arm may make the design legible, but the new wood is not evidence of the chair's manufacture. Leaving the gap visible preserves the boundary between old and new while obscuring the intended symmetry. Neither action is neutral; each directs attention toward one kind of historical claim. Visitors may reasonably want to know how a chair once looked and how it came to look as it does now. These are different questions, and a display that answers one well may leave the other harder to answer. The restorer cannot avoid the choice merely by invoking authenticity, because that term may refer to original material, original appearance, or the accumulated history of use. Before selecting a treatment, the institution must say which claim it intends the object to support and what evidence the treatment might remove from view.

The difficulty becomes clearer when an object has been altered during use. The chair in this example was made with short legs, later raised on blocks, and eventually cut down again. A restorer who selects the first state as the authentic one must remove evidence of its subsequent life. Yet the modifications may reveal more about the household's changing needs than the original design does. Calling them damage settles an interpretive question by vocabulary rather than argument.

Some curators respond by insisting that no intervention is acceptable. That rule is too simple as well. Unstable joints may cause further loss, and a protective treatment can preserve evidence that otherwise would disappear. The relevant distinction is not intervention versus nonintervention, but whether an intervention is documented, justified, and, where possible, reversible. A removable support can stabilize an object without pretending to be original. A digital reconstruction can show a proposed earlier state without requiring the physical object to embody it.

The museum should therefore explain what each display allows a visitor to infer. A reconstructed arm may be useful as an interpretation of form if it is visibly identified as reconstruction. The surviving chair can remain evidence of manufacture and later use without being forced into a single ideal moment. Conservation does not eliminate interpretation. Its responsibility is to keep interpretation from silently replacing the evidence on which future interpretations might depend.
